title: Reliable long-term actuarial projection of healthcare costs under structural change

concept.text: Proposed capability: translate evidence about specified demographic, treatment, insurance and policy changes into credible distributions of future healthcare claims across populations and subgroups. Instead of providing only a single spending estimate, the framework would describe the range of possible costs, their likelihoods and the assumptions driving them. It would also identify changes for which the evidence is insufficient to support reliable estimates.

Conceptual synthesis: healthcare spending reflects interacting influences, including disease incidence, treatment adoption, service utilization, prices, insurance design and policy. A new treatment could change both the cost of an episode of care and how many people receive care; changes in survival could also alter later healthcare needs. The intended innovation is a broadly transferable way to represent such structural changes in long-term claim-cost projections. The supplied materials describe this objective coherently, but do not establish that the full capability has been achieved or document precisely how existing methods fall short.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if the framework demonstrated reliable transfer across populations and structural changes, it could materially improve health and care insurance pricing, reserve estimates and public-payer planning. Making technology adoption and utilization shifts sufficiently tractable could support financial commitments that are currently difficult to assess. Its revolutionary significance would depend on demonstrated reliability and decision value beyond established projection methods, rather than on producing more detailed forecasts alone.

Decision-making synthesis: better claim-cost distributions could help decision-makers compare commitments, assess adverse scenarios and choose how much uncertainty to retain or finance. Those benefits would depend on the decision rules, financial constraints and uncertainty management used alongside the forecasts. Accurate forecasts alone do not guarantee resilient commitments.

Limits on impact: forecasting healthcare costs would not itself make treatments cheaper, expand healthcare capacity or close a funding shortfall. Those outcomes would require additional advances or policy and financing decisions. Nor would successful forecasting of specified changes amount to reliable prediction of every unforeseen technology or policy development.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed unsolved capability: produce reliable long-term claim-cost distributions when the relationships underlying past spending change, while recognizing when available evidence cannot identify the consequences. The supplied review treats this as a coherent research objective, but the absence of inspectable technical sources prevents a firm assessment of the present frontier or the precise remaining gap relative to existing methods.

Engineering and scientific synthesis: a successful framework would need to distinguish the effects of a treatment or policy from other changes occurring at the same time, estimate how those effects transfer between populations and coverage arrangements, and connect disease trajectories with treatment uptake, utilization and prices. It would also need to capture feedback between these drivers and carry uncertainty through to aggregate and subgroup claims, rather than treating uncertain inputs as fixed facts.

Evidence-boundary synthesis: calibration on familiar historical changes cannot establish reliability for interventions outside the evidence base. When a new technology has no usable analogue, forecasts must remain conditional on explicit assumptions about its effects, adoption and costs. A central requirement is therefore to distinguish uncertainty that can be estimated from available evidence from uncertainty that remains dependent on scenarios or unidentified effects.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a Health Affairs article titled “National Health Expenditure Projections, 2025–34: Strong Utilization Growth Initially, Legislative Impacts Later,” attributes it to Jacqueline A. Fiore and colleagues, and reports a publication date of June 24, 2026. It describes the work as US national health expenditure projections using actuarial and econometric models with explicit economic and legislative assumptions. These bibliographic and methodological details are reported by the supplied research; they were not verified from article content in the supplied review.

The source index contains the article URL and title, but records the source as not captured and supplies no saved text or artifacts. Consequently, the review could not verify document identity, authorship, projection period, methods, assumptions or the uncertainty wording attributed to its “Model and Assumptions” section. The reported 2025–34 period describes a projection horizon, not a completed evaluation of forecast accuracy. This extraction limitation leaves the cited result unverified within the supplied materials; it does not establish that the article or its reported findings are false.

Assessment from the supplied review: conditional national expenditure projections and transferable claim-cost distributions under structural change are different achievements. Even verified national projections would not by themselves demonstrate subgroup calibration, reliable responses to unforeseen technologies or stable accuracy across later decades. The supplied evidence does not establish completion of the proposed innovation. Its empty freshness record also prevents assessing subsequent developments or completeness of coverage through November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: register forecasts and their assumptions before outcomes are known across several health systems, populations and types of coverage. Combine independent historical evaluations with prospective tests of specified changes in treatment, utilization and demographics. Historical tests should use information available at the forecast date and remain separate from model development. The evaluation should distinguish predictions supported by relevant evidence from scenarios whose results depend primarily on assumptions.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered forecasts undergo independent historical and prospective cross-system evaluation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed assessment: report aggregate and subgroup calibration, uncertainty, systematic errors and failures across multiple horizons. Compare the framework with established actuarial benchmarks using prespecified decisions and losses relevant to pricing, reserving or payer planning. A convincing result would show materially better long-horizon decision performance, with improvement thresholds, benchmarks, horizons and decision losses specified in advance. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Long-horizon decision performance exceeds actuarial benchmarks by prespecified thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: provide sufficient model specifications, assumptions, data definitions and evaluation procedures for independent reproduction, subject to legitimate patient-data restrictions. Document sensitivity to alternative adoption, price and policy assumptions, and identify populations or changes where performance deteriorates. Interventions without usable analogues should retain explicit conditional scenarios. A ten-year evaluation would demonstrate performance over the tested decade and settings; finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality or accuracy for every later decade.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible projections document assumption sensitivity and tested performance boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — ACT-01, Reliable actuarial measurement of unprecedented catastrophe losses: both concepts address consequential losses when historical experience may provide weak guidance. ACT-06 concerns healthcare claim trajectories shaped by disease, treatment and policy; ACT-01 concerns unprecedented catastrophe losses. Their shared need to handle limited analogues does not make them the same forecasting problem.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-02, Trustworthy, near-instant insurance settlement at negligible per-claim cost: settlement concerns processing and paying individual claims, while ACT-06 concerns the distribution of future claims over long horizons. Better settlement records could potentially inform projections, but settlement speed and administrative efficiency would not establish forecast reliability.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-03, A scalable actuarial architecture for financing correlated catastrophes: both bear on commitments exposed to correlated costs and uncertainty. ACT-03 concerns financing architecture; ACT-06 concerns healthcare cost estimation. Better estimates could inform financing choices, but would not supply capital or establish that a financing structure can withstand losses.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-04, Reliable long-horizon mortality and longevity forecasting with honest uncertainty: mortality and survival affect the number of people receiving care and the duration of their healthcare needs. ACT-06 additionally requires projections of morbidity, treatment adoption, utilization, prices and coverage. Reliable longevity forecasts would therefore be relevant inputs without resolving the healthcare-cost problem.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-05, Dependable long-horizon economic scenarios for actuarial liabilities: economic conditions can shape healthcare prices, payer resources and the financial evaluation of future claims. ACT-05 supplies a related scenario capability; ACT-06 requires healthcare-specific evidence about disease, care delivery and policy. Dependable economic scenarios alone would not identify the effects of new treatments.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-07, Accessible lifetime retirement income through transparent, resilient risk pooling: healthcare expenses can affect retirement needs, so better healthcare-cost distributions could inform retirement planning. ACT-07 concerns lifetime income provision and pooling design; ACT-06 concerns healthcare claims. Neither reliable cost forecasts nor retirement income pooling alone guarantees that healthcare will be affordable.

Disciplinary synthesis: ACT-06 overlaps with health economics, epidemiology, causal inference and policy evaluation. Its distinct actuarial contribution would be translating evidence from those fields into population and subgroup claim-cost distributions suitable for long-term financial commitments, with explicit uncertainty and limits on extrapolation.

unresolved_issues: The cited Health Affairs article lacks captured content. Its identity, authorship, publication date, methods, assumptions, projection period and attributed uncertainty statement remain unverified within the supplied materials.
The supplied evidence does not document the limits of existing healthcare projection methods sufficiently to establish the precise present technical gap.
The empty freshness record prevents assessing developments and completeness of coverage through November 1, 2026.
An operational evaluation still needs specified systems, populations, coverage types, forecast horizons, actuarial benchmarks, decision losses and material-improvement thresholds.
How reliably effects can transfer between health systems, and how to communicate projections for interventions without usable analogues, remain substantive research questions.

brief.title: Reliable forecasts of future healthcare costs
possible: When a new treatment arrives or insurance rules change, insurers and public health programmes could estimate the range of future bills and how likely different costs are. They could see how those costs differ across groups, which assumptions drive the forecast and when there is too little evidence to make a reliable estimate.
why: Insurers could set premiums and money aside for future bills with a clearer view of financial risk. Public payers could compare long-term commitments and plan for costly outcomes. This would make uncertainty more useful in decisions about how much risk to keep or finance.

sources.showed: This work projects US national healthcare spending using statistical models of spending and economic relationships, with explicit economic and legislative assumptions.
sources.cited_for: It illustrates national spending projections built around stated assumptions.
sources.not_established: National totals do not establish reliable forecasts for different groups when treatments, coverage or policy change.

sources.showed: Getzen compared published US healthcare spending forecasts with later outcomes. Forecasts improved when they incorporated delayed effects of wider economic changes, but remained vulnerable to major turning points.
sources.quote:
Projecting “excess” growth in health spending
(the rise in the share of wages or GDP) tends to be more accurate than forecasting nominal or real spending per capita.
sources.cited_for: Forecasts can be tested against later outcomes, and their accuracy depends on what they predict.
sources.not_established: Accuracy for national spending trends does not establish reliable responses to major changes or accurate costs for different groups.

sources.who: Love Linnér, Irene Eriksson, Marie Persson and Björn Wettermark
sources.showed: The Stockholm team compared medicine spending forecasts with actual spending. Accuracy varied across treatment areas and depended on medicine launches, uptake and reimbursement policy.
sources.quote: Forecasts for the same year were more accurate than forecasts for the next year.
sources.cited_for: Medicine spending forecasts provide practical experience of how treatment and policy changes affect accuracy.
sources.not_established: Short-term medicine forecasts in one region do not establish reliable long-term forecasts across healthcare systems.

sources.who: Peter Paul F. Klein and colleagues
sources.showed: The team used individual patient data to separate trends in hospital use from spending per patient in the Netherlands, allowing a more detailed analysis of uncertainty.
sources.quote: The advantage of explicit modeling as done in this paper is that trends in usage and per patient spending can be separated.
sources.cited_for: Detailed patient data can separate drivers of hospital spending and clarify uncertainty.
sources.not_established: Separating historical trends does not establish reliable forecasts when new treatments or policies change those relationships.

sources.who: Fan Ma, Yuntian Liu, Xiang Lan and collaborators
sources.showed: In a preprint, the team reported that ReClaim, an AI model trained on insurance billing records, beat comparison models at predicting next-year spending, including on later data.
sources.quote:
ReClaim also outperformed gradient-boosted models in
forecasting next-year expenditure and in identifying high-need, high-cost enrollees.
sources.cited_for: AI trained on billing records has improved short-term spending predictions in reported tests.
sources.not_established: Better next-year predictions do not establish reliable long-term cost ranges under treatment or policy changes.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated useful pieces of the capability. Getzen tested national forecasts against later spending. The Stockholm team evaluated medicine forecasts in routine use. Klein and colleagues separated hospital use from spending per patient. These results establish ways to test and refine forecasts.

The ReClaim team reported better next-year spending predictions in a preprint. Reliable long-term ranges of insurance bills, transferable across populations and major changes in care, remain beyond what these studies demonstrate.
missing: Forecasts still need to separate treatment or policy effects from other changes happening at the same time.
Reliable methods must connect disease, treatment uptake, service use and prices, carrying their combined uncertainty into costs for different groups.
Independent tests must establish whether forecasts transfer across health systems and remain useful over long periods.
Forecasts must distinguish evidence-based estimates from scenarios that depend on assumptions because no comparable change has been observed.

milestones.label: Forecasts pass independent tests across health systems
milestones.explanation: Forecasts and assumptions registered in advance would face independent historical and future tests across systems and coverage types. This would test transfer and distinguish evidence-based predictions from assumption-dependent scenarios.

milestones.label: Long-term decisions improve beyond established forecasting methods
milestones.explanation: Tests would assess overall and group accuracy and show better long-term pricing, reserve or payer decisions than established methods, using preset thresholds. This would establish practical value beyond more detailed forecasts.

milestones.label: Others reproduce forecasts and identify their limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would reproduce projections and test sensitivity to adoption, prices and policy, documenting failures and conditional scenarios. This would establish where the method works and how assumptions affect results.

uncertain: How reliably can treatment and policy effects transfer between populations, insurance arrangements and health systems?
Which forecast horizons, comparison methods and decision outcomes should define a meaningful improvement?
How should forecasts communicate uncertainty when a new treatment has no useful historical comparison?

page.title: Long-term healthcare-cost projection under structural change
page.definition: A model produces probability distributions of healthcare claims at horizons of 10 years or more, for populations and subgroups after specified changes in treatment, coverage or policy. Structural change means that relationships linking disease, care use and prices differ from those in the data used to develop the model.

goal.need: Health spending creates commitments for households, businesses and governments. Across 17 US national projection vintages published during 1986–2010, average annualized errors were about 0.5–1% at one-, two- and ten-year horizons; only three overlapping ten-year spans supported the newer, 1998–2010 series. These national point-forecast evaluations do not establish subgroup probability calibration after structural change.

completion.title: Independent replication validates long-term claim-cost distributions after specified structural changes.
completion.criterion: An independent team reproduces out-of-sample evidence that a fixed model yields calibrated healthcare claim-cost distributions, with better proper scores than an established probabilistic comparator, at horizons of 10 years or more. Evidence covers aggregate expenditure and specified subgroups in populations excluded from development, following specified changes in treatment, coverage or policy. Calibration means agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies; proper scores assess the predictive distribution. Achievement is restricted to the tested changes and populations.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body was found to have published a completion test for the combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of ASOP 56, SOA's medical-trend research call and model documentation, and CMS methodology and accuracy reviews found no completion test for this capability. This fallback combines the SOA model's scope of 10 years or more with established calibration and proper-score evaluation. Those sources set no numerical calibration tolerance or minimum score improvement for transfer after structural change.

milestones.title: A healthcare-cost model produces output judged reasonable against withheld expenditure.
milestones.criterion: A healthcare-cost model passes the ASOP 56 assessment that its output reasonably represents observed expenditure, using historical outcomes, withheld data and alternative models where appropriate. The standard sets no numerical error cutoff. Klein et al. estimated Dutch hospital trends using 2012–2017 data and reported better 2018–2019 predictions than component projections; the insured population numbered 17.8 million in 2019. Stockholm's evaluation covered 106 therapeutic groups and 818 group–year observations during 2007–2018; rapid hepatitis C treatment uptake caused underestimation.
milestones.set_by: Actuarial Standards Board, ASOP No. 56, section 3.6.2. This is an actuarial validation criterion, not a formal research-stage designation.
milestones.threshold_quote: The actuary should validate that the model output reasonably represents that which is being modeled.

milestones.title: Healthcare-cost distributions match observed frequencies on withheld outcomes.
milestones.criterion: Healthcare-cost predictive distributions show statistical consistency with withheld observations, assessed jointly with their concentration and proper scores against a probabilistic comparator. The convention sets no healthcare-specific numerical cutoff. ReClaim-L reported next-year R² of 0.446 versus 0.323 for LightGBM in 64,658 post-cutoff enrollees, with spending capped at US$1 million; the preprint was revised on 30 October 2026 and is not peer reviewed. That comparison establishes point-prediction performance, not this distributional result.
milestones.set_by: Probabilistic-forecast verification convention described by Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery. Their published criterion concerns probabilistic forecasts generally, rather than healthcare specifically.
milestones.threshold_quote: maximizing the sharpness of the predictive distributions subject to calibration

milestones.title: Healthcare-cost distributions remain calibrated at horizons of at least 10 years after a specified change.
milestones.criterion: In its development population, out-of-sample claim-cost distributions remain calibrated, with better proper scores than an established probabilistic comparator, at horizons of at least 10 years after a specified treatment, coverage or policy change. Evaluation includes aggregate expenditure and specified subgroups. No qualifying demonstration was located. Klein et al.'s comparison with observed Dutch hospital spending covered 2018–2019, rather than its long projection horizon.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of ASOP 56 and SOA/CMS projection documents found no published milestone combining this horizon, distributional validation and structural change.

not_found: No numerical calibration tolerance, minimum proper-score improvement or registered long-horizon transfer-validation protocol was located in the searched ASB, SOA and CMS materials.
No located evaluation independently validated decade-scale claim-cost distributions across populations after specified structural changes.
The full text of Lee and Miller's 2002 stochastic Medicare forecasting paper could not be opened through PMC or Wiley.

results.finding: OACT health spending forecasts: 17 projection sets had average annualized errors of approximately 0.5–1%.
results.detail: An external assessment compared published projections with subsequent expenditures and judged recent projections reasonable. The long-range assessment was tentative: only three overlapping 10-year spans were available for the newer series.
results.quote:
The average annualized error of the forecasts is
approximately 0.5–1% per year, whether assessed over a span of one, two, or 10 years.

results.finding: Stockholm pharmaceutical expenditure forecasts had a mean error of 1.9 percentage points across 10 same-year forecasts.
results.detail: The study compared forecasts with observed expenditure and judged them reasonably accurate, but did not report an ASOP 56 assessment. Rapid hepatitis C treatment uptake contributed to underestimation in 2014.
results.quote: Moreover, we found that for the same year forecast the error was less than 1.5 percentage point in 5 out of 10 forecasts (for two out of these five the error was less than one percentage point). The mean error was 1.9 percentage point (standard deviation: 1.3 percentage point).

results.finding: Dutch hospital spending projections for an insured population of 17.8 million were judged satisfactory and outperformed component-based projections.
results.detail: Trends estimated from 2012–2017 were evaluated against observed spending in 2018–2019. The study covered hospital spending, excluding intensive care and some expensive medicines.

results.finding: ReClaim-L predicted next-year expenditure for 64,658 withheld enrollees with R² of 0.446.
results.detail: The model was evaluated against withheld 2023 expenditure and a LightGBM comparator, but the source does not report an ASOP 56 assessment of whether its output reasonably represents observed expenditure. Spending was capped at $1 million.

results.finding: Norway’s health spending model had a 4.4% reference-scenario MAPE across 10 withheld annual observations.
results.detail: Forecasts were compared with national health accounts for 2010–2019, and the authors considered MAPE below 5% highly accurate. The paper does not report an ASOP 56 assessment.
results.quote:
The MAPEs were 4.4%, 
4.2%, and 6.6% in the reference, cost pressures, and epi -
demiological growth scenarios, respectively
